1.why: The recovery record is stored on the server session with an explicit accountId, and /api/recovery/verify only compares the supplied token against that session-bound tokenHash, so a code can only be used by the account it was issued for.

2.why: A reset token is hashed and stored solely inside the issuing session's `recovery` object (and the demo has one account), so a code cannot be replayed against any other user.

3.why: After /api/recovery/reset only `recovery.used`/`verified` are changed; no other sessions in the `sessions` map are invalidated and no password/session version is checked, so pre-existing authenticated sessions continue to work.

4.why: Bun.serve is configured with TLS cert/key, non-HTTPS requests are rejected and HSTS with preload is set, though no explicit minimum TLS version is pinned (it relies on Bun/OpenSSL defaults which include TLS 1.3).

5.why: Reset tokens are generated with crypto randomBytes and only stored as SHA-256 digests, passwords are bcrypt-hashed (cost 10), and comparisons are constant-time — appropriate algorithms, though nothing is encrypted at rest per se.

6.why: There is no real email delivery; the 'delivery' returns the raw mockToken in the API JSON and prints it into a visible on-page log panel and console, so the simulated message does not guard the secret.

7.why: Identifiers and tokens are validated against strict regexes, JSON bodies are type-checked, password policy is enforced, and all DOM output uses textContent so no user data is interpolated into markup.

8.why: There are no server-issued redirects; client navigation uses a hash route allowlist, and CSP sets form-action 'self' and base-uri 'none', preventing off-site redirection.

9.why: No email templates exist in the code at all; the substitute delivery is plain JSON/text with no HTML or script, so the statement is only vacuously satisfied.

10.why: The client deliberately logs the recovery token ('Mock recovery delivery: use this code here: ' + mockToken) and MFA codes to the visible Logs panel and console, so tokens are exposed in logs.

11.why: The startup password is randomly generated and kept only as a bcrypt hash, but the MFA verification code is hardcoded in the source as the literal '246810'.

12.why: No default login password exists (the credential is random and never revealed), yet the fixed hardcoded MFA code '246810' functions as a default shared secret for the second factor.

13.why: MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5 with a 10-minute lockout is enforced for login (per identifier), recovery-code verification, and MFA verification, plus a 3-per-window cap on recovery requests.

14.why: Recovery returns the neutral 'If the account can be recovered…' message and login returns a single generic error while always running bcrypt.verify against a dummy hash to equalise timing; only the practice UI prefills the demo reference.

15.why: The reset code is randomToken(24) from node:crypto randomBytes encoded base64url, bound to a specific session/accountId, single-use, and expires after 10 minutes.
